Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology, natural history, and physical examination findings of
nonosteoblastic osteosarcoma subtypes.
Describe rare subtypes of osteosarcoma based on radiographic and histologic findings.
Perform a complete workup for a patient with osteosarcoma.
Review treatment options for osteosarcoma, including chemotherapy and surgical treatment
options.
Overview
Primary sarcomas of bone are exceedingly rare and represent as many as 0.2% of all
malignancies. Among these tumors, osteosarcoma is the most common.

Several different subtypes of osteosarcoma exist based on histologic and radiographic
appearance.1
Conventional osteoblastic osteosarcoma is the most common subtype and represents
approximately 70% all osteosarcomas.2
This lesson reviews nonosteoblastic osteosarcoma subtypes, including chondroblastic
osteosarcoma, fibroblastic osteosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma of bone
(UPS), telangiectatic osteosarcoma, small cell osteosarcoma, and giant cell–rich osteosarcoma
(GCR-OS; Video 1 ).
Video 1 Decilveo AP, O’Connor I, Wittig JC: Malignant Bone Forming Tumors: Osteosarcoma
and its Anatomic and Histologic Variants [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/18343__Videos.
Accessed July 9, 2021.
Epidemiology
Osteosarcomas have a bimodal age distribution.
Nonosteoblastic osteosarcomas represent approximately 30% of osteosarcomas.
Nonosteoblastic high-grade subtypes of osteosarcoma mainly are chondroblastic and
fibroblastic.
The other rare subtypes of non-osteoblastic osteosarcoma include UPS telangiectatic
osteosarcoma, small cell osteosarcoma, and giant cell osteosarcoma.


Epidemiology
Most cases of osteosarcoma occur in individuals in their teenage years. The second
major peak occurs in older adults—older than 65 years— and more commonly
secondary to conditions, such as Paget disease, prior radiation therapy, or bone
infarcts.3,5 Nonosteoblastic osteosarcomas represent approximately 30% of
osteosarcomas. The most common subtypes are chondroblastic (10%), fibroblastic
(10%), and other rare subtypes (10%). 
Subtypes of osteosarcoma include high-grade and low-grade variants, with prognosis
being closely related to tumor grade. The subtypes discussed in this lesson are all high-
grade nonosteoblastic variants.
UPS of bone, previously known as malignant fibrous histiocytoma, accounts for 2% to 5%
of bone sarcomas; as many as 25% of the cases are secondary to other conditions, such
as bone infarct, irradiation, and Paget disease of bone. UPS of bone also may present as
the dedifferentiated part of a dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma.
Telangiectatic osteosarcoma is reported to account for 2% to 12% of all osteosarcoma
cases.6 Clinically, a higher incidence of pathologic fracture is observed in patients with
telangiectatic osteosarcoma (as high as 25%). Radiographically, these tumors tend to
present with lucency and thinning of the cortices rather than an ossified background.
Minimal to no periosteal bone formation is observed, and expansile remodeling with a
wide zone of transition is noted. On MRI, they have a cystic appearance, with fluid-fluid
levels commonly observed. Overall, these features may resemble an aneurysmal bone
cyst.7,8
Small cell osteosarcoma is another rare subtype, which represents 1% to 2% of cases.
Demographics and age distribution are similar to that for other subtypes of
osteosarcoma. Small cell osteosarcoma is associated with a slightly poorer prognosis,
and patients usually present with pain. Radiographically, the lesion has little to no matrix
production, which is not typical for osteosarcoma.

GCR-OS is observed in skeletally immature patients who have a giant cell tumor with a
periosteal reaction.5 Another clue to differentiate GCR-OS from giant cell tumor of bone
is location: GCR-OS typically is found in the diaphysis, whereas giant cell tumor of bone
usually is metaphyseal and epiphyseal.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Most osteosarcomas occur in the appendicular skeleton.
Osteosarcomas in the axial skeleton are more common in the second peak (individuals in their
forties or older).
Classically, osteosrcomas occure near the metaphyseal growth plates of the long bones. Fifty
percent occur about the knee, with the distal femur being the most common anatomic
location, followed by the proximal tibia and the proximal humerus.
Patients with osteosarcoma in axial skeleton usually have a poorer prognosis because of
delayed diagnosis, a higher incidence of metastasis on presentation, older age group, inability
to tolerate aggressive chemotherapy because of age, and less effective surgical treatment
options for primary site control.9
Etiology
The true etiology is largely unknown, and the biology of osteosarcoma is particularly complex.

Etiology
Chromosomal instability and genetic heterogeneity are extremely common, with
considerably variable and complex karyotypes.10 Although usually the result of sporadic
mutations, the most common genetic abnormality is the alteration in cell cycle
progression checkpoint proteins (tumor suppressors). Loss of function of RB1 and TP53
transcription factors are the most common mutations in osteosarcoma patients. These
proteins participate in G1 to S progression of the cell cycle.
Risk Factors

9/4/26, 10:06 AM
AAOS | Nonosteoblastic Osteosarcoma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000542
4/16

Individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 mutation) and Rothmund-Thompson syndrome
(RECQL4 mutation) have a higher risk for osteosarcoma in their lifetime.
Other conditions that have been described to be risk factors for bone sarcomas are a history
of radiation therapy, Paget disease of bone, bone infarct, and chronic osteomyelitis.3,9,12
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The most common findings in patients with osteosarcoma are pain and swelling, which usually
are present for months.

Patient History
The pain usually is dull, constant, and exacerbated by activity. Patients may or may not
have a history of trauma. Pain is commonly experienced at night or at rest. Rarely,
patients present with a pathologic fracture. Other important points in the patient history
are genetic conditions and the presence of risk factors associated with secondary
osteosarcoma.
Physical Examination
Loss of range of motion, tenderness and swelling are the main findings in patients with
osteosarcoma of the extremities.
Symptoms such as fever, fatigue, or unintentional weight loss are not common.

Physical Examination
The affected area may be more swollen compared with the contralateral side. A palpable
mass may be present. Limited range of motion and tenderness to palpation also may be
present. A detailed neurovascular examination always is indicated. Depending on the
location of the tumor, extraosseous extension, and proximity to neurovascular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:06 AM
AAOS | Nonosteoblastic Osteosarcoma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000542
5/16

structures, motor or sensory alterations may occur.
The vascular examination usually is normal because blood flow can be preserved by
collateral flow.
Imaging Studies
The most appropriate initial imaging study is orthogonal radiographs of the affected bone.
MRIs with contrast of the entire affected bone and chest CT scan are essential for initial
staging.

Imaging Studies
Initial evaluation requires biplanar radiographs of the entire affected bone. Cross-
sectional imaging studies are then obtained to further characterize the lesion. CT usually
is easily available and can provide valuable information on the presence of
mineralization, cortical integrity, minimally displaced pathologic fractures, and articular
involvement.
MRI, with and without contrast, will provide additional details about soft-tissue
involvement; intramedullary and intra-articular extension; and valuable anatomic
information, such as proximity to and/or involvement of neurovascular structures. The
MRI must include the entire affected bone to rule out skip metastasis. To complete
staging during the initial evaluation, bone scintigraphy is performed to evaluate for
skeletal metastasis, and a CT chest scan is obtained to evaluate for pulmonary
metastasis.11
Pathology
Differentiating subtypes of high-grade osteosarcoma is based on the predominant matrix
being made by the tumor.


Pathology
Chondroblastic osteosarcoma is osteosarcoma with cartilaginous differentiation.
Microscopically, different stages of chondroid differentiation will be observed. After
mineralized, the chondroid tissue will show a blue background similar to
chondrosarcoma, with cellular-appearing hyaline cartilage. The difference is the
presence of pleomorphic atypical spindle cells with osteoid matrix production.3,5
Chondroblastic osteosarcoma is associated with poorer response to chemotherapy and
a higher incidence of metastases12 (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Images show chondroblastic osteosarcoma of proximal tibia. A, Histologic
image shows pleomorphic atypical spindle cells with osteoid matrix production in a
chondroid background (hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×20). AP (B) and lateral (C)
knee radiographs demonstrate a mineralized proximal tibia lesion. (Courtesy of Ali
Zarezadeh, MD, Gainesville, FL, and Andre Spiguel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Fibroblastic osteosarcoma is histologically dominated by atypical spindle cells
resembling fibroblasts with little bone matrix. The presence of osteoid and
pleomorphism differentiates this tumor from fibrosarcoma of bone (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Images show fibroblastic osteosarcoma of the distal femur. A, Histologic image
shows atypical spindle cells resembling fibroblasts with little bone matrix (hematoxylin-
eosin, magnification ×20). AP knee radiograph (B) and coronal T1-weighted knee MRI (C)
show a medial distal femoral lesion. (Courtesy of Ali Zarezadeh, MD, (Gainesville, FL, and
Andre Spiguel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
UPS of bone is characterized by lack of differentiation, considerable pleomorphism, and
lack of molecular markers. Recent retrospective studies revealed that almost 20% of
cases previously classified as fibrosarcoma of bone can be reclassified as UPS of
bone13,14 (Figure 3.
Figure 3 Images show undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma of bone. Hematoxylin-
eosin histologic images obtained at magnification ×10 (A) and magnification ×40 (B) show

a mixture of atypical fibroblasts and pleomorphic undifferentiated cells arranged in a
predominantly storiform fashion. C, AP knee radiograph demonstrates a radiolucency of
the proximal tibia. D, Axial T1-weighted, fat-suppressed, contrast-enhanced MRI of the
tibia shows a lesion inferior to the tibial tubercle. Lateral (E) and anterior (F) view
intraoperative photographs of the leg show allograft reconstruction performed with the
use of three-dimensional navigation. G, AP knee radiograph demonstrates the final
fixation construct. (Courtesy of Ali Zarezadeh, MD, Gainesville, FL, and Andre Spiguel,
MD, Chicago, IL.)
Histologic evaluation of telangiectatic osteosarcoma reveals blood-filled cystic spaces,
similar to an aneurysmal bone cyst; however, the difference is in the cystic septa and
lining. IN telangiectatic osteosarcoma atypical pleomorphic malignant spindle cells are
observed within the septa (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Images show telangiectatic osteosarcoma of the proximal humerus. A,
Histologic image shows blood-filled cystic spaces in an osseous background and septae
with atypical spindle cells (hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×20). B, Coronal T1-weighted
shoulder MRI with contrast shows an enhancing lesion of proximal humerus. C, AP
shoulder radiograph demonstrates radical resection of the proximal humerus and
endoprosthetic reconstruction. (Courtesy of Ali Zarezadeh, MD, Gainesville, FL, and
Andre Spiguel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Histologic evaluation of small cell osteosarcoma reveals round cells with hyperchromatic
nuclei. The osteoid matrix formation is rare and, if present, very course. Therefore,
Ewing sarcoma and other tumors of the small, round cell family are included in the

9/16

differential diagnosis for small cell osteosarcoma. Although the cells in small cell
osteosarcoma may be CD99 positive, the presence of EWS gene rearrangement is
diagnostic for Ewing sarcoma and must be evaluated because of differences in
management of the diseases8,15 (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Images show small cell osteosarcoma of the proximal fibula. A, Histologic image
shows small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in an osseous background
(hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×20). T1-weighted coronal (B) and axial (C) knee MRIs
with contrast and AP (D) and lateral (E) knee radiographs show a lesion with little to no
matrix production. AP (F) and lateral (G) knee radiographs demonstrate radical resection
and proximal tibiofibular joint stabilization. (Courtesy of Ali Zarezadeh, MD, Gainesville,
FL, and Andre Spiguel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Although the presence of multinucleated giant cells in osteosarcoma is not uncommon,
very rarely GCR-OS may become dominant and obscure the malignant sarcomatous
background. Histologically, sheets of giant cells with a mononuclear background are

observed; however, within this background, atypical mitotic activity and many nuclear
atypia are observed (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Histologic image shows a giant cell rich osteosarcoma. Note the presence of
multinucleated giant cells in an osseous background with atypical spindle cells
(hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×20). (Courtesy of Ali Zarezadeh, MD, Gainesville, FL,
and Andre Spiguel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Management
The most common treatment option for high-grade osteosarcomas is neoadjuvant
chemotherapy, after which radical resection of the tumor is performed and followed by
adjuvant chemotherapy.
No difference in survival has been reported after amputation versus limb-salvage procedures.
Endoprosthetic reconstruction is the most common method of reconstruction in limb salvage
procedures.
Allograft and autograft reconstruction are associated with a higher rate of revision surgery.
Nonsurgical Management
If left unmanaged, osteosarcoma is a lethal disease. Before the introduction of modern
chemotherapy in the 1970s, the prognosis for patients with osteosarcoma was poor. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:06 AM
AAOS | Nonosteoblastic Osteosarcoma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000542
11/16

current treatment options for all discussed subtypes of osteosarcoma consists of neoadjuvant
chemotherapy and wide surgical resection, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy.
The most frequently used regimens are based on high-dose methotrexate, doxorubicin, and
cisplatin.
With such management, the rate of 5-year disease-free survival is almost 70%. Despite
advancements in chemotherapeutic agents, the prognosis has not changed for osteosarcoma,
and survival has plateaued.1 Multiple ongoing clinical trials are attempting to identify
molecular targets and potential better treatment strategies to improve survival in patients with
osteosarcoma.16,17
The presence of more than 90% necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a good
prognostic indicator with regard to survival;18 however, changing the chemotherapeutic
regimen postoperatively for poor tumor necrosis does not affect overall survival.
Surgical Management
The goal of surgical management of osteosarcoma is to achieve local control. For extremity
sarcomas, surgical treatment options include amputation versus limb salvage. Although
amputation used to be the standard treatment option for osteosarcoma, it currently is rarely
performed. Given the advancements in surgical and reconstruction techniques over the past
few decades, limb salvage is more common.12 Overall, no difference in survival is noted
between these two groups if a wide resection is performed with negative margins and
standard chemotherapeutic management is undertaken.19 A recent study reported better
overall survival in patients who underwent limb salvage surgery.20
Reconstruction options for limb salvage mainly are allograft, occasionally with added
autograft, versus endoprosthesis.
The advantage of endoprosthetic reconstruction is immediate–weight bearing with modular
implants that are off-the-shelf. It also usually is less technically challenging, and outcomes are
more predictable (Video 2).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000542
12/16

Video 2 Sonnylal L, Hoskins T, O’Connor I, Sampat R, Wittig JC: Radical Resection of Proximal
Tibia Osteosarcoma [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21603__Videos. Accessed July 9, 2021.
Allograft reconstruction often requires an extended period of non–weight bearing to allow for
healing of the allograft-host junction. The risk of nonunion per junction is approximately 15%,
with the diaphyseal junction failing more frequently. The infection rate also is slightly higher in
allograft reconstruction compared with endoprosthetic reconstruction.21
Outcomes of allograft reconstruction and endoprosthetic reconstruction are similar. The
incidence of revision surgery is higher after allograft reconstruction.
A considerable number of patients with osteosarcoma are children of growing age. Skeletally
immature patients will continue to grow after reconstruction, which must be considered.
Expandable endoprostheses and rotationplasty should be considered in patients with lower
extremity sarcomas. Epiphysiodesis in the contralateral extremity also may be necessary to
minimize limb-length discrepancy.
Regardless, a detailed discussion should occur between the patient and the treating surgeon
with regard to different options, what each option entails, expectations, outcomes, and
possible complications.

Outcomes
The rate of 5-year disease free survival for patients with localized osteosarcoma and no
evidence of distant metastasis is 70%.
Despite modern chemotherapy and successful resection, the 5-year survival of patients who
experience local recurrence or distant metastasis ranges from 10% to 20%.

Outcomes
Patients with pulmonary oligometastatic disease may benefit from metastasectomy or
radiation therapy. In some patients, systemic chemotherapy may be considered;
however, no consensus exists with regard to an optimal regimen. The most common
surveillance methods are extremity radiographs and chest imaging studies (chest
radiographs or CT scans) in 3- to 6-month intervals for a duration of 5 years.1,22-24
Mark as Complete
